title: Arjuna Drops His Bow
hookLine: Arjuna sets down his bow, and Krishna answers with Nani's line
carry: karma yoga: the act is yours, the fruit isn't
tomorrow: why would anyone turn down half a fortune?
last: WRITING GOD'S NAME IS A PRAYER.

cards: Two armies face each other on a field called Kurukshetra. The conch shells have sounded. Arjuna, the finest archer alive, asks his charioteer to drive out between the lines so he can see who he's about to fight.
His charioteer is Krishna. And there they are: his teachers, his cousins, old Bhishma, the grandsire who watched him grow up. Arjuna's hands shake.
His great bow slips from his grip. He sits down in the chariot and says: I will not fight.

teach.h: YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE ACTION.
teach.b: What Krishna says next fills the eighteen chapters of the Bhagavad Gita.
Deep into chapter two, once Krishna has shown him who he really is, comes the line Priya is copying for Nani: your right is to the action, never to its fruits.
Don't let the fruit be your reason for acting, and don't cling to doing nothing either.

teach.h: KARMA YOGA: THE PATH OF ACTION.
teach.b: This is karma yoga, the path of action, one of Hinduism's great ways to God. Karma means action, and in Hindu teaching actions leave traces that bind a person to the round of birth and death. So should Arjuna just stop?
No, says Krishna: no one can stop acting, even for a moment.
What binds isn't the act. It's clinging to what you'll get from it. So do your dharma, your rightful work, the way an offering is made: with full care, then let it go.
Later Krishna says it plainly: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, do it as an offering to me.
Many Hindus live this in small ways: work begun with a prayer, the first of a meal set before God, the result left in God's hands. Priya, at her desk, meets the line one curl at a time.

The word for the right is adhikara, and in its syllable dhi the short i's curl is drawn in front of the letter, though it's said after. She draws it slowly, and notices she's stopped worrying whether Nani will cry.

teach.h: THE ACT IS YOURS. THE FRUIT ISN'T.

how: Many Hindus offer their work and its results to God, with a short prayer before starting or by setting the first of a meal before the home shrine; teachers often point to the Gita's karma yoga as the reason.

o: the script Nani's line from the Gita is printed in
the language Krishna and Arjuna fight in

p: sets down his bow: I will not fight

s: Krishna tells Arjuna to stop acting so his karma stays clean
no one can stop acting even for a moment, he says. what binds is clinging to the fruit.
Nani's line comes from Krishna's answer to Arjuna
it's from chapter two of the Gita, Krishna's answer after Arjuna says he won't fight.
karma yoga means not caring how your work turns out
you work with full care; you just don't make the fruit your reason, and you offer it.

games.q: your aunt sets the first bit of every dish aside for God and says the cooking 'isn't really hers'. by Krishna's teaching, what's she doing?
o: karma yoga: doing the work with care and offering its fruit.
being modest, so no one criticizes the food.
a superstition to keep the dish from burning.
games.why: whatever you do, Krishna says, do it as an offering to me. the work is hers; the fruit is given away.

practice: Pick one small task you'll do after this: washing a cup, sending a message. Before you begin, offer it. If you pray, say in your own words, this is for you, the way Krishna asks; if you don't, name who it serves.
Do it with care. When it's done, notice the pull to check how it landed, and let that go on the out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Devanagari: the script Nani's line is printed in, where adhikara, the right, carries a curl that's drawn first and said second.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a right, a claim; in the Gita's line, your right is to the action. Its dhi has the short i's curl drawn first.

carryVoice: For the road: karma yoga. The act is yours; the fruit isn't. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.20–47 (Arjuna sees his kin; the bow slips, 1.29; he sits down, 1.47)
